case_studies.abstract: Malware analysis demands rapid interpretation of complex detonation reports spanning filesystem, network, and process behaviours. While large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive capabilities for technical artifact interpretation, the opacity and escalating API costs of closed-weight frontier models motivate exploration of open-weight alternatives. However, many open-weight models are large, demanding significant compute resources and incurring non-trivial hosting costs that place them beyond reach for resource-constrained deployments. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of costly and resource-intensive malware analysis by building an orchestrated ensemble of small, open-weight language models, resulting in better performance than single large language models. The researchers built a system that combines the strengths of multiple small models to outperform larger models. This is relevant to IT work as it can help reduce costs and improve malware analysis capabilities.

case_studies.title: CodeRescue: Budget-Calibrated Recovery Routing for Coding Agents
case_studies.abstract: Coding agents increasingly operate in executable environments where a failed attempt produces actionable feedback rather than merely an incorrect answer. Existing cost-aware systems typically treat such failures as cascade decisions: try a cheap model first, then escalate hard cases to a stronger and more expensive model. In coding, however, execution feedback can also make further cheap-model recovery worthwhile, raising a budgeted deployment question: when should an agent spend more cheap compute, and when should it escalate? case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of efficiently allocating resources for coding agents when they encounter failures, by building a system called CodeRescue that determines when to use cheaper models for recovery and when to escalate to more expensive ones. The result is a more budget-aware approach to coding agent deployment. This research does not directly impact cloud infrastructure management.

case_studies.title: PoTRE: Test-Time Reasoning inspired by Cognitive Heterogeneity

case_studies.title: Notes to Self: Can LLMs Benefit from Experiential Abstractions?
case_studies.abstract: Humans distill experience into reusable abstractions, e.g., strategies and cautionary reminders, and apply them to gradually solve problems more effectively. We study whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly benefit from such experiential abstractions. From LLMs' solution traces on the MATH training set, a stronger teacher or the LLMs themselves extract natural-language abstractions into a retrievable library. case_studies.summary: This research explores if Large Language Models (LLMs) can benefit from experiential abstractions, similar to how humans learn from experience. The team built a library of natural-language abstractions extracted from LLMs' solution traces and tested two usage modes. The result shows that these abstractions can improve LLM performance.

case_studies.title: IteraSim RAG: A Multi-Stage Retrieval-Augmented Agentic Back-End for OpenFOAM-Based Computational Fluid Dynamics
case_studies.abstract: Configuring a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) case in OpenFOAM requires assembling a multi-directory input deck of mutually consistent solver, discretisation and boundary-condition dictionaries -- a task that remains a substantial barrier to non-specialist use of open-source CFD software. Large language models (LLMs) coupled with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can lower this barrier, but existing systems retrieve with a single flat query, apply one retrieval strategy to operationally distinct requests, and let a single agent both draft and review its own output. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of configuring computational fluid dynamics cases in OpenFOAM by building a multi-stage retrieval-augmented agentic back-end. The result is a system that can help non-specialists use open-source CFD software more easily. This research does not directly impact day-to-day cloud infrastructure management work.

case_studies.title: LKValues: Aligning Large Language Models with Sri Lankan Societal Values
case_studies.abstract: Value alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) has been shown to be culturally biased toward Western norms. This results in the mishandling of local values in multilingual societies such as Sri Lanka that have their unique cultural dynamics. Existing benchmarks overlook Sri Lankan-contextualized values in its official language Sinhala, hindering culturally sensitive evaluation and fine-tuning. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of cultural bias in large language models by creating a resource suite called LKValues, which aligns these models with Sri Lankan societal values. The result is a more culturally sensitive evaluation and fine-tuning of language models for multilingual societies like Sri Lanka. This research is specifically focused on natural language processing and not directly applicable to cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it relates to natural language processing and cultural bias in AI models. Otherwise, no immediate action is required for cloud infrastructure management.

case_studies.title: Sound Probabilistic Safety Bounds for Large Language Models
case_studies.abstract: We propose a novel framework for computing rigorous bounds on the probability that a large language model (LLM) generates harmful output to a given prompt. We study a new application of the Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals to obtain probably approximately correct (PAC) bounds for this problem. The researchers built an algorithm that prioritizes exploring branches in the auto-regressive generation tree to efficiently compute lower bounds. The result is a more efficient way to identify potentially harmful outputs from large language models.

case_studies.title: PyroDash: Cost-Efficient Token-Level Small-Large Language Model Collaborative Inference
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide strong reasoning capabilities but are expensive to serve at scale, whereas small language models (SLMs) are cheaper but less reliable on difficult problems. We introduce PyroDash, a cost-aware framework for token-level SLM-LLM collaborative inference. During generation, the SLM decides whether to request assistance by emitting a control token. A Collaborate Engine then sends the query and partial reasoning trace to a frozen LLM for completion through a single handoff. The policy is internalized in the SLM, requiring neither a separate router, LLM retraining
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of expensive large language models by building a cost-aware framework called PyroDash, which enables collaboration between small and large language models to improve reasoning capabilities at a lower cost. PyroDash allows small language models to request assistance from large language models when needed. The result is a more cost-efficient approach to language model inference.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for AI or machine learning workloads, here is what to do: review your current language model deployment costs, consider implementing PyroDash to optimize costs, and assess the potential benefits of collaborative inference for your organization.
case_studies.score_reasoning: No clear actionable steps provided for IT engineers or consultants to apply this framework within 90 days.

Parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) are frequently used to reduce computational costs. The result is a more efficient way to fine-tune language models without requiring large amounts of data or computing power.
